narrative:
The model determined that you have a 72.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class ranking in the third year of law school was the strongest influence. You placed in the bottom decile (1 out of 10), far below the average of roughly the middle of the class among accepted students. This low ranking strongly pushed the prediction toward failure.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor. At 23.5, it sits well below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted. This weaker performance also increased the model’s estimate of your risk of failing the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. At 2.6 it is below the accepted students’ average of 3.23, yet the model still saw this as a mildly positive signal that slightly reduced the predicted chance of failure. Unfortunately, this small encouraging effect was not nearly enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your third-year ranking and LSAT score.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT. Strengthening these two areas would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction.
